subject: math
cluster: Understand the concept of a function and use function notation
description: Students determine whether a relation between two sets is a function, where a function from a domain to a range assigns to each input exactly one output. They identify the domain and range of a relation given as a set of ordered pairs, a table, a mapping diagram, or a graph; apply the vertical line test to graphs; interpret function notation $f(x)$ as the output corresponding to input $x$ (and evaluate $f$ at given inputs); and recognize that the graph of $f$ is the graph of the equation $y = f(x)$.
subSkills: Decide whether a relation (set of ordered pairs, table, or mapping diagram) is a function by checking that each input has exactly one output
Apply the vertical line test to decide whether a graph represents a function
State the domain and range of a relation given as ordered pairs, a table, a mapping, or a discrete graph
Interpret function notation: read $f(x)$ as the output of $f$ at input $x$, and distinguish input from output
Evaluate a function at a numeric or symbolic input from a rule, a table, or a graph
Connect a function to its graph: the graph of $f$ is the set of points $(x, f(x))$, i.e. the graph of $y = f(x)$, so $f(a)=b$ corresponds to the point $(a,b)$

problemArchetypes.name: Function-or-not from ordered pairs
problemArchetypes.example: Is the relation $\{(1,3),(2,5),(3,7),(2,9)\}$ a function? Explain. (No: the input $2$ is paired with both $5$ and $9$.)

problemArchetypes.name: Vertical line test on a graph
problemArchetypes.example: A graph shows a parabola opening to the right (a sideways parabola $x = y^2$). Does the graph represent a function? (No: a vertical line crosses it twice.)

problemArchetypes.name: Domain and range of a relation
Interpret function notation
problemArchetypes.example: If $g(x)$ gives the cost in dollars of $x$ tickets, what does $g(4)=52$ mean? ($4$ tickets cost $\$52$.)

problemArchetypes.name: Read a value from a table or graph
problemArchetypes.example: From the graph of $y=f(x)$, the point $(2,7)$ lies on the curve. Find $f(2)$. ($f(2)=7$.)

problemArchetypes.name: Mapping diagram classification
problemArchetypes.example: A mapping diagram sends $1\to a$, $2\to a$, $3\to b$. Is it a function? (Yes: each input maps to exactly one output; outputs may repeat.)

Easy.description: Single-step identification or evaluation from an explicitly given representation. Student checks the one-output-per-input rule on a short list of ordered pairs or a small mapping, reads domain/range off a finite set, or evaluates a linear rule at a positive integer. The correct representation is fully shown; no setup or interpretation of context is required.
constraints: Relations given as 3 to 4 ordered pairs or a 3-element mapping diagram
Function-or-not cases are unambiguous (a repeated input is plainly visible, or all inputs are clearly distinct)
Evaluation uses a linear rule $f(x)=ax+b$ with small integer coefficients and a positive integer input
Domain/range asked only for finite, discrete sets
These items anchor the start of the single worksheet and form the lower half of tier1

Medium.description: Requires reading a less direct representation or doing light computation. Includes the vertical line test on a continuous graph, evaluating at negative or fractional inputs, evaluating quadratic or absolute-value rules, or interpreting function-notation statements in a real-world context. One layer of reasoning beyond a direct lookup.
constraints: Vertical line test applied to continuous graphs (line, parabola, circle, sideways parabola)
Evaluate rules such as $f(x)=x^2-3$ or $f(x)=|x|+2$ at negative or non-integer inputs (e.g. $f(-2)$, $f\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)$)
Translate between $f(a)=b$ and the point $(a,b)$ on the graph of $y=f(x)$
Interpret the meaning of a function-notation statement in context
These items occupy the middle of the single worksheet; they form the top of tier1 and the bottom of tier2

Hard.description: Multi-step or abstract: determine for which value of a parameter a relation becomes (or fails to be) a function, evaluate at a symbolic or algebraic input, combine representations, or justify a conclusion with the domain/range/exactly-one-output definition. Requires extracting information and chaining two or more ideas.
constraints: Solve for an unknown coordinate so that a relation is (or is not) a function, e.g. find all $a$ making $\{(1,2),(a,5),(3,7)\}$ not a function
Evaluate at a symbolic input, e.g. given $f(x)=3x-1$ find $f(2k)$ or solve $f(x)=11$ for $x$
Use a graph plus the definition to identify domain and range of a continuous function over an interval
Justify with the definition why a vertical line test failure means a relation is not a function
These items close the single worksheet and form the upper half of tier2

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student thinks a function may not repeat OUTPUTS, so a relation with a repeated $y$-value is judged not a function
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Calls $\{(-2,4),(0,1),(3,4)\}$ not a function because $4$ appears twice as an output, when in fact repeated outputs are allowed

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student allows an input to map to two outputs, missing the exactly-one-output requirement
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Calls $\{(1,3),(2,5),(2,9)\}$ a function despite the input $2$ having two outputs

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses the vertical line test with the horizontal line test
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Concludes a parabola $y=x^2$ is not a function because a horizontal line meets it twice

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student swaps domain and range, listing outputs as the domain
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reports the domain of $\{(-2,4),(0,1),(3,4)\}$ as $\{1,4\}$ (the range) instead of $\{-2,0,3\}$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student reads $f(x)$ as multiplication, treating $f(3)$ as $f\cdot 3$
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Given $f(x)=2x-5$, computes $f(3)$ as $f\times 3$ or as $2-5\cdot 3$ instead of $2(3)-5=1$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses input and output, returning the input when asked for $f(a)$ from a graph
commonMisconceptions.distractor: From the point $(2,7)$ on $y=f(x)$ reports $f(2)=2$ instead of $f(2)=7$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student substitutes into the wrong variable or mishandles signs when evaluating
Student solves $f(x)=b$ by evaluating instead of solving for the input
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Asked to solve $2x-5=11$, reports $x=2(11)-5=17$ instead of $x=8$
